features.description: Long straight-line runs of unrolled copies of a short instruction sequence, with registers, memory offsets, or constants varying between copies.
Repeated call chains use `mov` to forward a call’s `rax` return value into `rdx` or `rsi`, then pass it with another operand in `rdi` to the next call.
Function epilogues restore several callee-saved registers with consecutive `pop` instructions, then tail-call through `jmp cs:xxx`.
A pointer held in a callee-saved register, commonly `rbx` or `r12`, is repeatedly moved into `rdi` immediately before a call, with the same pointer reused across helper calls.
The code loads pointer or object values from globals, stack slots, and base-plus-offset memory into general-purpose registers, then propagates those values into nearby call setup.
A dense sequence of calls with explicit SysV argument setup, repeatedly loading pointer arguments into RDI and RSI with MOV or LEA immediately before each call.
A long unrolled aggregate initialization using repeated `mov` instructions to store `CONST` immediates directly into memory slots or fixed-offset fields.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Long sequences of calls through `cs:xxx`, often with argument setup between calls and repeated calls within the same basic block.
Many branches lead to inline early-return cleanup stubs that restore the stack, pop saved registers, and execute `retn`.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Repeated helper-call setups load a `GLOBAL_VAR` address with `lea` into a SysV argument register and place immediate constants in other argument registers before the call.

Repeatedly reloads a pointer from a stack-local slot with `mov reg, [rbp+var]` or `mov reg, [rsp+var]`, then uses it for constant-offset memory accesses and passes the pointer or derived address in an argument register to a call.
Repeated call sites load an immediate value into ESI—the SysV second-argument register—before calling a function, often with a pointer or object in RDI.

The pattern is setting up high-arity calls by placing arguments in the SysV registers (`rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8`, `r9`) and pushing additional arguments onto the stack immediately before the call.
The code repeatedly uses `lea` to form `GLOBAL_VAR` addresses and passes them in call-argument registers, especially `rdi`, immediately before calls.
Repeated direct calls are set up by taking addresses of stack-resident locals with `lea` and passing those pointers in argument registers, commonly `rdi` and `rsi`.

Repeated SysV x86-64 variadic-call setup: arguments are loaded into the integer argument registers, then EAX is cleared or loaded with an immediate before CALL to supply the ABI’s AL vector-argument count.

A byte-sized Boolean/status result is kept in `AL`, tested to steer a conditional branch, then normalized into an integer return with `and al, imm` followed by `movzx eax, al`, often after `xor eax, eax`.
Long stretches of straight-line code repeat near-identical instruction templates, often adjusting a register or memory offset with `add` or `lea` between repetitions.
Repeated access to global function-pointer slots through `cs:xxx` operands, loading and dereferencing the pointer before dispatching through an indirect call.
A guarded reference-count release: the code decrements a memory-resident count, branches when it remains nonzero, and calls a hidden cleanup routine when the count reaches zero.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
A stack-canary check loads the saved value from a stack slot into `rdx`, executes `sub rdx, fs:xxx`, then conditionally branches on the result.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Helper-call sites commonly stage arguments from stack slots or stack addresses in `rsi` and `rax`, then pass the `rax` value in `rdi`, sometimes pushing additional arguments onto the stack.
Long unrolled runs repeatedly use `add reg, CONST`, often to advance a pointer or index between memory accesses and calls.
Helper-call return values are folded into a running count or offset with `add`, with the accumulator held in a stack slot and reused in nearby bounds checks or indexing.
The code repeatedly initializes or updates constant-offset object fields through a pointer in `RAX`, using stores such as `mov [rax+CONST], ...` around helper calls.
A cluster of `lea` instructions loads `GLOBAL_VAR` addresses into call-argument registers such as `rdi` and `rsi`—often also `rcx`, with `edx` set to a constant—immediately before a `call cs:xxx`.
Repeated switch-case stubs load a `GLOBAL_VAR` address with `lea` and unconditionally `jmp` to the same shared `JUMP_ADDR_n` target.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
A call through `cs:xxx` is preceded by setup of four SysV arguments: global addresses in `rdi`, `rsi`, and `rcx`, plus an immediate in `edx`.
The function ends with two consecutive `retn` instructions, often immediately after the stack-restoring `pop` sequence.
The functions commonly preserve the incoming third argument (`rdx`/`edx`) near entry in a stack slot or callee-saved register for later use across calls.
A `jnz JUMP_ADDR_n` follows subtracting the thread-local `fs:xxx` stack canary from a saved canary value loaded from a stack slot, forming a stack-protector check before stack teardown and return.
A pointer loaded from a memory field is checked with `test reg,reg` and a following `jz` before it is dereferenced or passed to a call.
The recurring pattern is accessing a fixed-offset field through a pointer in `rax`, using instructions such as `mov`, `movzx`, or `lea` with an operand of the form `[rax+CONST]`.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Incoming arguments are first spilled or staged in stack slots, then the `fs:xxx` stack canary is saved to the stack, followed by `xor eax, eax` to zero the return register.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
The code uses data-dependent guards, applying `test` or `cmp` to loaded fields and indices and then taking conditional jumps to control traversal or loop termination.
Repeatedly form addresses of stack-local temporaries with `lea`, pass them in `rdi` to helper calls, and often spill the address into another stack slot.
A stack-protected function saves `fs:xxx` into a local stack slot, then immediately zeroes `eax` with `xor eax,eax` before the main body.
Function-call setup uses `lea` to load a `GLOBAL_VAR` address into an argument register, notably `rsi` or `r9`, immediately before a `call`.
The functions save the high callee-saved registers, typically `r14`, `r13`, and `r12`, then restore them in reverse order with consecutive epilogue `pop` instructions.
Repeated calls pass the same saved object or context value in `rdi`/`edi` as the first SysV argument, while other arguments vary between calls.
The feature marks SysV x86-64 variadic-call setup, where EAX is set to the vector-argument count (often with `xor eax,eax`) immediately before the call, with overflow arguments pushed onto the stack.

A recurring pattern is an immediate arithmetic update followed by a zero/equality branch and a `lock`-prefixed operation whose result is checked with another conditional branch, forming an atomic retry/update sequence.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Repeated null-guarded cleanup calls load an object pointer into `rdi`, test it, branch past the call if it is null, and otherwise call a direct helper such as `sub_xxx`.
A callee-saved register is checked with `test reg,reg`, and the result immediately controls a zero/nonzero conditional jump.
After null-checking a pointer loaded from an object, compare the qword at that pointer’s address with a previously obtained pointer (`cmp [rax], rsi`) and branch on equality (`jz`).
The code commonly loads a stack-local value into ECX as the fourth System V integer argument, with the other argument registers set up around a nearby call.

The code mutates pointer-based data structures by following register-held pointers and writing computed values back through register-relative memory operands, commonly fixed-offset fields or bitmap words.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
The feature is in-body `xor`-based bit and condition handling: `xor` acts on working registers, often near `sub` or `test` instructions and conditional branches.
The functions commonly save `r12` first among the callee-saved registers with `push r12`, keep it live across calls, then restore it last with `pop r12` before returning or tail-jumping.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Repeated `add` instructions apply a constant or loaded offset to an argument register—especially `rdi` or `rsi`—to adjust a pointer or value before subsequent use.

A switch-style multiway dispatch repeatedly compares one scalar with immediate constants and branches to case blocks or a shared target using equality tests, signed or unsigned range checks, and a final unconditional jump.
The code frequently prepares a call by loading an immediate constant into `EDX` as the SysV third argument, then setting up `RSI` and `RDI` and calling the function.
A hash-table lookup zeroes `edx`, uses unsigned `div` to compute a remainder, then uses `lea reg,[base+rdx*8]` to address an 8-byte bucket slot.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
NO CLEAR PATTERN
NO CLEAR PATTERN
A 32-bit value is loaded from a memory operand into `r13d`, then carried into a later store or function call.
A call result in `rax` is saved to a callee-saved register and later passed as the first argument in `rdi` to another call.
A recurring pattern is passing the address of a stack-resident temporary or buffer to a call, typically using `lea reg, [rsp+...]` or `mov reg, rsp` to set an argument register.
A value is loaded from memory into a 32-bit argument register (`edi` or `esi`), often with `movzx`, and then passed to a nearby call.

An `endbr64`-prefixed tail block saves `rax` in a callee-saved register, compares memory or global data with an immediate to steer a conditional branch, then makes helper calls with object pointers loaded into `rdi`, often including the saved value.
Repeated call sites set up the fifth SysV x86-64 argument in `r8`—often with `lea` or `cmovz`—immediately before calling a helper.
A persistent object pointer is kept in callee-saved `r12` across calls, with repeated fixed-offset field accesses through `[r12+CONST]` and calls that pass `r12` in `rdi`.
Scalar SSE floating-point processing uses XMM registers to load values from stack slots, perform arithmetic or comparisons, and write results back to stack slots.
The function entry allocates a stack frame with `sub rsp, CONST` and spills the incoming `rdi` pointer into an `[rsp+...]` local for later reloads and dereferences.
The functions repeatedly chase pointer fields with dependent loads such as `mov rax, [rax+CONST]`, often spilling the loaded pointer to a stack slot before dereferencing it again.
Long straight-line runs of repeated function calls, with arguments reloaded into the SysV argument registers from object fields or `lea`-formed addresses before each call.
Repeated calls use the System V integer-argument registers, with unused argument slots explicitly zeroed by `xor reg, reg` and pointer arguments often loaded with `lea` before the call.

Repeated helper-call setup loads immediate constants into argument registers such as `esi` and `edx`, often alongside a `GLOBAL_VAR` address passed in another argument register.

Conditional validation of pointer-like values held in RAX, using `test` or `cmp` immediately before a flag-dependent jump.

Helper-call sequences repeatedly reload scalar fields from object, global, or stack memory into 32-bit general-purpose registers, then use those values in index arithmetic, tests, or subsequent call-argument setup.
Repeated calls are set up by loading a stack-object address into `rdi` and a `GLOBAL_VAR` address into `rsi` (often via `lea` and `mov`), then calling a helper.

Several functions contain out-of-line `endbr64` cleanup blocks that preserve a value in `rbx`, pass the address of an `rbp` stack local in `rdi` to a cleanup call, and then jump back to the main control flow.

The code repeatedly builds a stack-resident descriptor by storing `CONST` immediates alongside pointer or address values in `[rsp+...var...]` slots, then passes the descriptor’s address in an argument register to a helper call.
Repeated SysV AMD64 variadic-call setup, with `mov eax, CONST` immediately before a call to place the vector-argument count in `AL`.
Repeated helper-call sites use the SysV register convention, placing addresses of stack-local temporaries—often alongside a global address—in `rdi` and `rsi` immediately before `call`.
Repeated call setups use `lea rsi, GLOBAL_VAR` to pass a global-data address as the second argument, often in a dense series of similar calls.
Repeated helper calls load a 32-bit value into EDX and forward it to ESI as the second SysV argument, often with a stack-slot address in RDI as the first argument.
Multiple branch arms load an immediate status or return value into `eax` and unconditionally jump to the same shared continuation.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
A loaded 32-bit state value is repeatedly checked with `test reg,reg` and `cmp reg,imm`, with conditional branches guarding a `lock`-prefixed update that uses the same register.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Repeated call sites load a global address into the first SysV argument register (`lea rdi, GLOBAL_VAR`) and call a function, often testing the `eax` result to choose a conditional branch.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
A 32-bit integer argument is saved near function entry in a stack slot or callee-saved register, then carried across helper calls and conditional control flow.

Repeated zero-displacement `mov` accesses through a register-held object pointer—loading or storing its first word via operands such as `[rbx]`, `[rax]`, or `[r12]`, often using that word as a pointer.
A stack-protector check compares the saved stack canary with `fs:xxx`, conditionally jumps on a match, and calls the failure handler on a mismatch.
Repeatedly materializing internal function addresses with `lea reg, sub_xxx` and storing them into fixed-offset fields of an object or callback record.
After a call, the return value in `rax` is tested for zero with `test rax, rax`, and a `jz` or `jnz` branch follows.
A pointer held in `rsi` is repeatedly checked with `test rsi,rsi`, followed by a conditional `jz` or `jnz` before the code dereferences it or calls a function.
The code obtains object pointers from calls and initializes or updates fixed-offset fields through them with immediate values, computed results, and scalar or SIMD stores.
The functions repeatedly pass the value in `RDX` as the first argument to a call using `mov rdi,rdx`.
A pointer null/equality check feeds a `jz` branch, with the fall-through making a helper call—often after `lea rsi,[rax+CONST]`—then another call with `rdi` loaded from an object register.
Repeated interior `endbr64` blocks capture `rax` into `rbp` with `mov rbp, rax`, then pass `rbp` as the first call argument via `mov rdi, rbp`.

The code frequently initializes pointer-based structures by loading or checking a base pointer, then storing immediate constants or scalar values into fixed-offset fields with instructions such as `mov [reg+CONST], imm` and `mov [reg+CONST], reg`.
A single 8-byte stack-alignment slot is reserved with an early `push rax` or `push rcx` and discarded near the exit with `pop rdx`, just before a return or tail jump.
Calls through `cs:xxx` are followed by dereferencing the RAX result with `mov eax, [rax]` to fetch a 32-bit status value, often negating or testing it for error handling.
The code tests an 8-bit register against itself with `test`—for example, `al`, `bpl`, `cl`, `dil`, `dl`, or `sil`—to set flags used by a conditional jump or `cmov`.
Each function pushes `rax` before its call sequence, then later pops the stack slot into `rdx`.
A recurring pointer-chasing load: `mov rax, [rax]`, often dereferencing a pointer just loaded from a global or thread-local slot.
Repeated call-adjacent `mov rbp, rbx` instructions, often preceded by `mov rdi, rbp` to set up the call’s first argument.

A pointer-identity guard reloads a stack-held pointer, follows it with consecutive `mov rax, [rax]` loads, null-checks the intermediate value with `test`/`jz`, then compares the resulting pointer with a stack-held value and branches on mismatch.

Repeated internal `endbr64`-prefixed blocks save a preceding call’s `rax` result in a callee-saved register, call a helper with a stack/context pointer as an argument, then pass the saved result to another call.
The code materializes a local `sub_xxx` routine’s address with `lea` in a SysV argument register and passes it to a callee as a function-pointer callback.
A call’s return value in `rax` is forwarded as the first argument in `rdi` to a subsequent call, typically with `mov rdi, rax` before that call.
Many functions test the third argument with `test rdx, rdx` near the start, then immediately use a conditional jump to branch according to whether it is null.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Outlined `endbr64` blocks pass the address of a stack-resident temporary in `rdi` to a call, then pass a saved pointer in `rdi` to a follow-up call.
Repeated virtual-method dispatch through an object pointer in `r12`: load `[r12]`, fetch a function slot from that table, then transfer control indirectly through the loaded pointer.
Repeated call sites pass a pointer or context held in a callee-saved register by copying it into a later System V integer-argument register, typically `rcx` or `rdx`.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
A `push rax` reserves an 8-byte stack-alignment slot before a `call`, with the slot often discarded afterward using `pop rdx`.
The function saves `rbx`, copies the first argument from `rdi` into it, then uses `rbx` as an object base for offsetted field accesses across calls.
The code frequently compares a value at a zero-offset memory location, such as `[rax]` or `[CONST_VAR]`, with a constant or register and branches conditionally on the result.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
The code repeatedly treats `AL` as a boolean result, using `test al, al` followed by `jz`/`jnz` and sometimes storing or zero-extending that byte value.
NO CLEAR PATTERN
Repeated range checks compare a computed value with a limit using `cmp`, `comisd`, or `ucomisd`, then use a conditional branch or move based on the result.
A 32-bit count is incremented by an immediate, compared unsigned against an immediate limit, and sent by `ja` to an out-of-range target.

Dense stack spill/reload sequences shuttle many XMM registers, often including `xmm7`, through stack slots using `movdqa`, `movdqu`, `movaps`, and `movups`, interleaved with general-purpose register spills.
Repeated SSE/AVX dataflow uses `xmm0` as a working register, with arithmetic and lane-shuffle/packing instructions reading or writing it.
Repeated memory-processing loops use RCX as a cursor, advancing it by a fixed stride and comparing it with an endpoint.
A recurring pattern is incrementing a field at a register-based address with an immediate, typically `add [reg+CONST], CONST` after guard checks.
A stack-slot loop index is initialized from an immediate, incremented by a constant, and compared against a bound to control a conditional loop back-edge.
Repeatedly load a value from a `cs:xxx` global with `mov`, dereference it through `[rax]`, and feed the resulting value into a nearby call, often in `rdi` or `edi`.
Repeated helper-call sequences use `test al, al` or a pointer comparison to set flags, then a 64-bit `cmovcc` selects a pointer or global-address candidate for a subsequent call.

Repeatedly initialize or update pointer-rich records by computing field or element addresses with `lea` or scaled-index arithmetic, then storing register-held pointers into fixed-offset fields to create links between records.
The feature detects direct memory writes and read-modify-writes through register-based addresses, especially `mov [reg+offset], value` and `add [reg+offset], CONST` targeting pointed-to fields.
